SEC Charges Software Company and Executives in Revenue Recognition Scheme

Published 2026-10-05 18:00 UTC

The Securities and Exchange Commission today charged a publicly traded software company and three of its former executives with engaging in a scheme to improperly recognize revenue in order to meet analyst estimates over several quarters.

According to the SEC's complaint, the executives pressured sales staff to close deals before the end of each quarter by offering side agreements that gave customers the right to cancel or receive refunds. These terms were hidden from the company's accountants and auditors. As a result, the company recognized revenue it was not entitled to record under accounting rules, overstating revenue by about $94 million over two years.

The complaint alleges that the former chief executive and chief financial officer knew about the side agreements and signed false certifications attached to the company's periodic reports. A former sales vice president allegedly drafted many of the agreements and instructed staff to keep them out of the company's contract management system.

The company restated its financial statements last year after an internal investigation, and its stock price fell sharply. The SEC said the company cooperated with the investigation and took remedial steps, including replacing senior management and improving internal controls.

The company agreed to pay a $6 million civil penalty to settle the charges without admitting or denying the findings. The SEC's litigation against the three former executives is continuing in federal district court, where the agency is seeking disgorgement, civil penalties and officer-and-director bars.

The SEC thanked the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board for its assistance in the investigation, which was conducted by the Division of Enforcement's Issuer Reporting and Accounting group.

The SEC reminds investors that companies must recognize revenue only when they have satisfied their obligations to customers, and that executives who certify financial statements are responsible for their accuracy. The agency continues to prioritize cases involving financial reporting fraud.
